splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA and MPPAA require actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in as of the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as long as the assumptions are applied to data as of that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled while the supervisee is a fugitive, so that the period of absconding does not count toward completion of the supervised release term.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release during absconding and that the judicially-created fugitive tolling doctrine cannot extend punishment beyond the statutory term.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) against raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement on top of § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from re-raising claims.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to successive § 2255 motions by federal prisoners, who need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split affects the ability to challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that may affect the outcome of their election, recognizing competitive injury as sufficient.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge state election rules before an election merely based on speculative competitive harm.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under § 3553(f)(1) only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) is conjunctive, so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to an agency's or the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of an ambiguous provision that expands criminal liability or enhances sentences. The Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold lenity prevails.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor or Chevron deference when construing ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretation.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity when the Commission's commentary interprets an ambiguous guideline, even in the criminal sentencing context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether USSG Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) is entitled to deference under Kisor. This affects whether conspiracy convictions trigger the career-offender enhancement.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary is invalid — text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline and is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule is broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in USSG § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally scheduled. This matters for career-offender and other guideline enhancements based on prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) encompasses any offense under state law punishing the distribution or manufacture of a controlled substance, even if the substance is not federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal schedule limits — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction only qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines if the substance involved is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory life sentences for certain drug offenses, may contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as a factor — alone or in combination with others — supporting compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically bars such consideration, while other circuits allow it as one factor among many.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor among others in evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes categorically barred
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether offered alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, filed in connection with a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 30-day appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises from a criminal proceeding, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than civil rights actions (Bivens or § 1983) to challenge conditions of confinement or BOP decisions that affect the duration or terms of custody, including First Step Act time-credit disputes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement — as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment — must be brought via habeas corpus or may be pursued through civil rights actions. This affects federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits, transfer to prerelease custody, and similar issues.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that any challenge that effectively seeks earlier release or speedier transfer to prerelease custody must be brought through habeas corpus, not civil rights actions.

positions.label: Conditions-of-confinement claims may proceed as civil rights actions
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may be brought via civil rights actions rather than habeas.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A) allows good-faith converting debtors to retain appreciation in their assets that accrued between the petition date and conversion date. The outcome significantly affects debtors' decisions about converting to Chapter 7 and the availability of assets for creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to the property's value as of the original petition date, allowing debtors to keep post-petition appreciation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may impose a sentence upon revocation of supervised release that is intended to punish the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit, under its precedent in United States v. Lewis, allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits restrict revocation sentences to addressing the breach of the court's trust rather than independently punishing the violative conduct.

positions.label: Punishment for the violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that a district court may consider punishment for the underlying conduct when sentencing upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentences address breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be primarily aimed at sanctioning the breach of the court's trust inherent in the violation, not at punishing the defendant for the underlying conduct as if it were a new offense.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination liability in hospitality and service industries, suggesting the decision may resolve a circuit split on the applicable standards and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied legal standards for discrimination claims in the hospitality context that SCOTUS found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims by patrons of business establishments, creating the conflict that prompted certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker,' preempts state negligence claims arising from a freight broker's selection of a motor carrier. This question affects liability in the trucking industry where brokers play a significant intermediary role.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted because they relate to the broker's 'service' of arranging transportation, which falls within the FAAAA's preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent hiring of motor carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate brokers' prices, routes, or services within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to a person who uses marijuana.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users — particularly marijuana users — is consistent with the Second Amendment's text and historical tradition of firearms regulation.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) does not violate the Second Amendment because the historical tradition of firearms regulation supports disarming individuals whose drug use renders them dangerous or irresponsible.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a sufficient historical analogue justifying the disarmament of non-violent drug users.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence — claims that might also be raised in a habeas petition under Section 2255 — as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under Section 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that could be raised in a § 2255 habeas petition — such as alleged legal errors in a conviction or sentence — can also be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A). Some circuits permit such consideration, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors in compassionate release analysis
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider potential legal errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, as there is no categorical bar on such consideration.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release to address habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the legality of a conviction or sentence belong in a § 2255 motion and cannot serve as the basis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
